explanation based on systematic guiding questions to facilitate
reflection and knowledge organisation, thereby deepening their
understanding and construction of the learning content. Across
the four stages of the model, self-explanation serves as a bridge

edge co-construction, ensuring that learners enter collaborative
phases with cognitively prepared and explicit representations.

Next, in order to deepen knowledge construction, this study
adopted the self-explanation-guided virtual museum learning
model, which allowed learners to complete self-explanation
tasks in textual form through online structured guiding
worksheets (Figure 4). The core of the self-explanation strat-
egy was to motivate learners to externalise their own under-
standing of knowledge, which not only reduced the burden on
their working memory but also enhanced their participation
in the construction of meaning in the content, generating
clear and detailed descriptions of knowledge for themselves.
Specifically, this process required learners to organise and
reorganise content, making meaningful connections between
new information and existing knowledge. In this study, “con-
necting existing information with new concepts” was oper-
ationalised through artefact appreciation. Students already
possessed fragmented understandings from class and supple-
ments, for instance, knowledge of dynasty context and social
customs (e.g., the Tang dynasty's emphasis on burial items),
the symbolism of idioms (¢.g., #1, denoting many de-
scendants), and the evolution of scripts and inscriptions
(e.g., text cast on the inner walls of bronze vessels). In vir-
tual museum learning, learners were situated in an artefact
appreciation context. They activated and reorganised their
prior knowledge and then integrated it with new, artefact-
specific information via self-explanation tasks. The process
of translating understanding into words facilitated learners’
knowledge construction, and enhanced the retention and sub-
sequent transfer of knowledge.

Collaboration stage: Group members constructed a concept
map of knowledge through synchronous collaboration, shared
the results of their group discussions (Figure 5), presented their
work to the class, and received feedback and suggestions from
both peers and the teacher. The collaborative process not only
required members to organise and connect the core concepts
together but also facilitated the externalisation and sharing
of knowledge through visual images. Through collaborative
planning and practice, group members achieved collaborative
knowledge construction and deepened their systematic under-
standing of the content. Collaborative knowledge construction
at this stage benefited from the refined understanding and clar-
ification achieved during the conversation stage. Through the
scaffolding provided by the preceding construction and con-
versation stages, learners entered the collaboration phase with
sufficient cognitive readiness and a shared foundation of under-
standing. This enabled the final collaborative concept mapping
to proceed efficiently.

Through the scaffolding provided by the preceding construction and conversation stages, learners entered the collaboration phase with sufficient cognitive readiness and a shared foundation of understanding. This enabled the final collaborative concept mapping to proceed efficiently.

For the analysis of learning behaviour patterns, the learning
behaviour coding scale proposed by Hwang et al. (2023) was
used as a reference and was adjusted to fit the context of this
study. Based on the design of the virtual museum learning en-
vironment, the following eight behavioural codes were selected
and retained: start experience (SE), explore object (EO), repeat
object (RO), answer correctly (AC), wrong answer (WA), read
materials (RM), next scene (NS), and finish experience (FE).
The definitions and descriptions of these behaviours are shown
in Table 1. These codes were mainly used to classify the be-
haviours displayed by students during the process of completing
the learning tasks.

2. Fostering Critical Thinking

Students reported that the learning process fostered critical
thinking. This included the ability to promote diverse thinking.
Besides, the experimental group uniquely reported two abilities:
evaluating the accuracy of viewpoints and developing indepen-
dent thinking skills (Table 8). Most students in the experimental
group stated that before participating in facilitating collabo-
ration, they built their understanding and perspectives on the
content through the process of self-explanation, which involved
developing independent thinking skills. This process helped
them more effectively evaluate the accuracy of viewpoints
during group collaboration and provide constructive feedback.

3. Fostering Collaboration

In terms of facilitating collaboration, students mentioned sev-
eral aspects. These included the ability to communicate and
share opinions, as well as the ability to collaborate to complete
tasks. Besides, the experimental group additionally reported an
extra ability: achieving group consensus (Table 8). Most stu-
dents in the experimental group believed that after completing
the self-explanation task, they could express their viewpoints
more clearly when entering group discussions. Through com-
municating and sharing opinions, they were able to compare
and integrate different ideas, which helped them achieve group
consensus. In contrast, students in the control group often men-
tioned situations where they either omitted certain content or
struggled to explain their thoughts clearly.

4. Enhancing Metacognition

In terms of enhancing metacognition, students mentioned the
ability to develop and refine conceptual knowledge. Besides, the
experimental group solely reported two abilities: self-monitoring
comprehension and adapting learning strategies (Table 8). Most
students in the experimental group stated that when answer-
ing the self-explanation task questions, they were better able to
monitor their understanding of the learning content. They also
became more aware of the information easily overlooked during
the exploration of the virtual museum scenes, prompting them
to adapt their learning strategies and focus more on the key
information.

In terms of enhancing metacognition, students mentioned the ability to develop and refine conceptual knowledge. Most students in the experimental group stated that when answering the self-explanation task questions, they were better able to monitor their understanding of the learning content. They also became more aware of the information easily overlooked during the exploration of the virtual museum scenes, prompting them to adapt their learning strategies and focus more on the key information.

5. Increasing Learning Motivation

In terms of increasing learning motivation, students reported
two common willingness indicators: their willingness to apply
the approach to other courses and their willingness to continue
to use the approach. Besides, the experimental group exclusively
reported an additional aspect: the desire to explore the learning
content further (Table 8). E04 stated that this learning approach
sparked their interest in learning and made them curious about
the interdisciplinary knowledge embedded in the artefacts. It
also motivated them to proactively read the learning materials
first whenever entering a new scene. C05 expressed that the
learning method was very interesting, and they hoped to con-
tinue using it and apply it to different course content. Besides,
E08 mentioned that the museum collections contain many ar-
tefacts, but this learning activity only focused on a few items.
After completing the collaborative concept mapping with the
group, E08 expressed the hope to have more opportunities to ex-
plore additional artefacts in the future.

paragraphs: 5. Increasing Learning Motivation

In terms of increasing learning motivation, students reported two common willingness indicators: their willingness to apply the approach to other courses and their willingness to continue to use the approach. Besides, the experimental group exclusively reported an additional aspect: the desire to explore the learning content further (Table 8). E04 stated that this learning approach sparked their interest in learning and made them curious about the interdisciplinary knowledge embedded in the artefacts. It also motivated them to proactively read the learning materials first whenever entering a new scene. C05 expressed that the learning method was very interesting, and they hoped to continue using it and apply it to different course content. Besides, E08 mentioned that the museum collections contain many artefacts, but this learning activity only focused on a few items. After completing the collaborative concept mapping with the group, E08 expressed the hope to have more opportunities to explore additional artefacts in the future.
